title: Sugar in the iron bowl
hook: the Guru stirs water with a double-edged blade while reciting, and tradition says Mata Jito added sugar crystals

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Panj Pyare, the five beloved. Your line was daya, dharam, himmat, mohkam, sahib. Which one did you practice? Day eighty-six.

Almost every tradition marks the moment someone joins it with water. A baby at a font. A convert in a river. A pilgrim at a well. Water is how people say: something new begins here. On Vaisakhi, 1699, with the five beloved standing beside him and the crowd watching, the Guru called for an iron bowl and clean water. He didn't just pour it. He knelt, took up a khanda, a double-edged sword, and began to stir the water with the blade, round and round, while reciting hymns. It took a long time. And then, tradition says, someone stepped forward and added one more thing. Today, the water of the Khalsa.
screen: `WATER MARKS A BEGINNING.` → `AN IRON BOWL, A DOUBLE-EDGED BLADE.` → `SOMEONE ADDS ONE MORE THING.`

segments.voice: Amrit. The word means the nectar of immortality, literally not-death. You met it inside the name Amritsar, the pool of nectar, on day fifty-five. On Vaisakhi, 1699, amrit took on a new meaning: the sweetened water of Sikh initiation. Here's how it was made, as Sikh tradition tells it. Clean water in an iron bowl. The Guru stirring it with the khanda, the double-edged sword, while reciting five hymns, among them the Japji of Guru Nanak and the Anand, the song of bliss you met on day fifty-three. The bowl is iron, and the blade is steel: strength, courage, readiness. And then the sweetness. Tradition says the Guru's wife, Mata Jito, came with sugar puffs, patashe, and dropped them into the water. Some accounts name her Mata Sahib Kaur instead; the sources differ, and Sikhs tell it both ways. Either way, the meaning Sikhs draw from it is the same. The blade alone would make the water hard. The sugar alone would make it soft. Together, strength and sweetness. The Khalsa was to be brave, and also gentle. Firm, and kind. A soldier who serves langar. Then the Guru gave the amrit to the five, sprinkling it on their eyes and hair and giving it to them to drink, all from the same bowl, men of different castes drinking together. That was the point too. The same practice continues today. It's called amrit sanchar, and five initiated Sikhs, standing as the Panj Pyare, prepare the amrit in the same way.
screen: `AMRIT — NECTAR OF IMMORTALITY.` · `THE KHANDA STIRS, HYMNS ARE SUNG.` · `MATA JITO ADDS THE SUGAR.` · `ONE BOWL, EVERY CASTE.` · then, large: `STRENGTH AND SWEETNESS.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: add something sweet to plain water. If you can, pour a glass of water. Add a little sugar, or honey, or a slice of fruit, and stir it slowly, watching it dissolve. As you stir, think of one place in your life where you've been all strength and no sweetness, or all sweetness and no strength. Then drink slowly, and let the two come together. If you can't get water right now, just picture it. The bell holds the time.
Amrit. The nectar of immortality; for Sikhs, the sweetened water stirred with a double-edged sword, given at initiation.
Your line: strength and sweetness. Today, when you have to be firm with someone, be kind in the same breath. Day eighty-six.

screen: `DAY 86 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: THE GURU BECOMES THE DISCIPLE.`

howItsDone: Sikhs who choose to be initiated take amrit in a ceremony called amrit sanchar, where five initiated Sikhs prepare sweetened water in an iron bowl, stirring it with a khanda while reciting five banis.

fork.setup: you're preparing the water of initiation. it's been stirred with a double-edged blade. what do you add?
fork.reveal: tradition says sugar puffs were added: strength from the blade, sweetness from the sugar, together.

original.note: Punjabi, in Gurmukhi, from Sanskrit amṛta: not-death, the nectar of immortality.

trapdoor: what it means: water stirred with a blade and sweetened with sugar, strength and gentleness together, shared from one bowl.
what a scholar hears: Sanskrit a-mṛta, not-dead; the ceremony is khande di pahul, the initiation of the double-edged sword.

notes: Who added the patashe: the index names Mata Jito; many accounts name Mata Sahib Kaur (Mata Sahib Devan). The script gives both without choosing. Confirm.
The five banis (Japji, Jaap, Tav-Prasad Savaiye, Chaupai, Anand Sahib) are named only in part (Japji and Anand). Confirm.
Assumes Amritsar (day 55) and Anand (day 53) were taught; confirm references.
Sprinkling on eyes and hair and drinking from one bowl follows the rite as described in tradition and the Rehat Maryada; confirm.
Opening line about water marking a beginning in many traditions is a general neighbor note; confirm it does not read as comparison.
